source.title: Integral points on Markoff type cubic surfaces
readSections: The entire arXiv v3 (30 May 2022, 55 pages; §§1–10, Appendices A–B, references), read 2026-09-22. PDF https://arxiv.org/pdf/1706.06712v3, SHA-256 e4ddc7a115ad4afd61f0063d0b931baf85792eee2267d1d5c232bece11d3163d. The authors state that v3 is the final version; the published version has an abridged §10 and "some additional differences". The published PDF is paywalled and was not available, so locators are v3 page numbers.

summary: Studies the integral points on the Markoff level surfaces V_k : x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k. Γ-descent with a new function Δ gives explicit fundamental sets for the orbits of the Markoff group Γ (Theorem 1.1), so the class numbers h(k) are finite and computable. Local solubility holds exactly when k ≢ 3 mod 4 and k ≢ ±3 mod 9 (Proposition 6.1). Quadratic reciprocity gives infinitely many Hasse failures, ≫ K^{1/2}(log K)^{−1/2} of them (Theorem 1.2(i), Propositions 8.1–8.3). A variance argument over moving planes shows that almost every admissible k is represented, with Zariski-dense integral points (Theorem 1.2(ii)). It combines Blomer–Granville bounds, the δ-method for quaternary quadratic forms and explicit local densities (Appendix B). The paper also treats Zariski density and the perfect, universal forms U₁ and U₂, averages of h(k) (§7), and computations to 5.6×10⁸ with conjectures (§10). Twenty source issues are recorded (one added at review); none affects Theorem 1.1 or Theorem 1.2(ii). The atlas has the Markoff descent (CA.4, via PAPER-MARTIN-25), the Markoff-action Part II, local densities (ES.3, planned) Mathlib's reciprocity, Gauss sums and Hensel lemma, and the Fricke trace identity (planned in Tau Ceti BelyiMaps Layer 4). It has none of the level-k theory, the almost-all theorem or the explicit densities.

items.name: Affine forms, their level sets V_{k,F} and v_F(k)
items.statement: An affine form in n variables is f ∈ ℤ[x₁,…,x_n] whose leading homogeneous part f₀ is non-degenerate (no linear change of variables writes it in fewer than n variables) and such that f − k is absolutely irreducible for every constant k. For k ∈ ℤ, V_{k,F} = {x : F(x) = k} and v_F(k) = |V_{k,F}(ℤ)|.
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Admissible values; perfect, almost perfect and full forms
items.statement: k is admissible for f if V_{k,f}(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for every prime p (no congruence obstruction). f is perfect if V_{k,f}(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_{k,f} for all but finitely many admissible k; almost perfect if this holds for almost all admissible k (natural density); full if v_f(k) → ∞ as k → ∞ along almost all admissible k. For an affine form the admissible k are given by congruence conditions ([LW54], [Sch76]).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: The Markoff cubic M and its level surfaces V_k
items.statement: M(x) = x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ and V_k = V_{k,M} : M(x) = k for k ∈ ℤ (1.4), (2.1). Changing the sign of one coordinate identifies V_k with x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = k (9.6). V₀(ℤ) is {(0,0,0)} together with the triples 3·(Markoff triples); V₄ is the singular Cayley cubic.
items.note: The coefficient-one normalisation. PAPER-MARTIN-25 uses the coefficient-three equation x²+y²+z² = 3xyz; the two are related by x ↦ 3x at k = 0 only. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: The Markoff group Γ and narrow equivalence
items.statement: Γ is the group of polynomial affine transformations of 𝔸³ generated by the Vieta involutions V₁(x) = (x₂x₃ − x₁, x₂, x₃), V₂(x) = (x₁, x₁x₃ − x₂, x₃), V₃(x) = (x₁, x₂, x₁x₂ − x₃), the permutations of the coordinates and the changes of sign of two coordinates. Γ preserves M, hence each V_k(ℤ). Narrow equivalence uses only permutations and double sign changes.
items.locator: §1, p.3; §2, p.9; §4.1, p.13, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (misprint E4 in the formula for V₂)
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Class numbers h_M(k) and h^±_M(k)
items.statement: For k ≠ 4, h_M(k) is the (finite) number of Γ-orbits in V_k(ℤ), with h_M(k) = 0 if V_k(ℤ) = ∅. h^±_M(k) = |F^±_k(ℤ)|, where ± = sgn(k) and F^±_k are the fundamental sets of Theorem 1.1; h^±_M(k) = h_M(k) for generic k and h_M(k) ≤ h^±_M(k) otherwise.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Admissible, exceptional and generic k for M; Hasse failures
items.statement: k is admissible for M iff k ≢ 3 (mod 4) and k ≢ ±3 (mod 9) (Proposition 6.1); there are 7K/12 + O(1) admissible 0 < k ≤ K. k is exceptional if V_k(ℤ) has a point with some |x_j| ∈ {0, 1, 2}; equivalently k = u² + v², 4(k − 1) = u² + 3v², or k − 4 = u² with u, v ∈ ℤ. The remaining admissible k are generic; every admissible k < 0 is generic. A Hasse failure is an admissible k with h_M(k) = 0; exceptional k are never Hasse failures.
items.note: The count of exceptional k is the Landau-type bound in the AN.5 item. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 2.1 (descent for k > 4) and the cases 1 ≤ k ≤ 3
items.statement: If k > 4, every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a point of the finite set S⁺(k) ∪ T(k), where S⁺(k) = {(−x₁, x₂, x₃) : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = k} ∩ ℤ³ and T(k) is the finite set of solutions with a coordinate 0 or 1; otherwise it is narrowly equivalent to a point with 3 ≤ x₁x₂ − x₃ < x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁ ≥ 3, to which a Vieta move applies. V₃(ℤ) = ∅; V₂(ℤ) is the infinite Γ-orbit of (0, 1, 1); V₁(ℤ) is the finite orbit of (0, 0, 1).
items.note: Revisits the descent of Markoff [Mar80], Hurwitz [Hur07] and Mordell [Mor53] without the height |x₁|+|x₂|+|x₃|. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 2.2 (descent for k < 0)
items.statement: For k < 0 every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a point of S⁻(k) = {3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2} ∩ V_k(ℤ) ⊆ U(k) = {3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ √(|k| + 9), 3 ≤ x₃ ≤ 3(|k| + 9)/2}; points of V_k(ℤ) never have a coordinate in {0, ±1, ±2}; and for |k| large x₁ ≪ |k|^{1/3}, x₂ ≪ (|k|/x₁)^{1/2}, x₃ ≪ (|k|x₁)^{1/2}.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: The Δ-function from Bhargava cubes
items.statement: For x ∈ ℤ³ the three Bhargava slicings of the cube with entries 1, x₁, x₂, x₃ ([Bha04]) give binary quadratic forms Q_i(u, v) = (x_jx_k − x_i)u² + (1 + x_i² − x_j² − x_k²)uv + (x_jx_k − x_i)v² with common discriminant Δ(x) = (1 + x₂² − x₁² − x₃²)² − 4(x₁x₃ − x₂)² = (1 + x₁ + x₂ + x₃)(1 + x₂ − x₁ − x₃)(1 + x₃ − x₁ − x₂)(1 + x₁ − x₂ − x₃) (3.1). Δ ≡ 0 or 1 (mod 4) as x₁² + x₂² + x₃² is odd or even; Δ is invariant under permutations and double sign changes; if 2 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ then Δ < 0 iff x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁ + x₂ − 2.
items.note: Only the polynomial Δ is used later; the cube is motivation. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: The case k = 0: (3.2) and Markoff's two orbits
items.statement: V₀(ℤ) consists of the two Γ-orbits of (0, 0, 0) and (3, 3, 3) ([Mar80]); Δ(0,0,0) = 1, Δ(3,3,3) = −80, and on V₀(ℤ) one has Δ(x) < 0 iff x = (3, 3, 3) up to permutation and double sign change (3.2). So Δ attains a unique minimum on each orbit, at its root.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: The Δ-differences (4.1) and the orbit tree
items.statement: On V_k, with Δ_i = Δ ∘ V_i: Δ₁(x) − Δ(x) = x₂x₃(x₂x₃ − 2x₁)[2(k − 5) + (x₂² − 4)(x₃² − 4)], and cyclically for Δ₂, Δ₃ (4.1). The brackets are positive for generic k ≥ 5 and for all k < 0 (using (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) = (2x₃ − x₁x₂)² − 4(k − 4)). Hence in the Vieta graph modulo narrow equivalence a positive node (x₁, x₂, x₃), 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, has two neighbours with larger Δ and one with smaller Δ, and a negative node (−x₁, x₂, x₃) has three neighbours with larger Δ. For k < 0 a point has no Δ-smaller neighbour iff it lies in S⁻(k).
items.locator: §4.1, (4.1) and Figure 6, pp.13–14; §4.2, p.14, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 1.1 (fundamental sets)
items.statement: (i) Let k ≥ 5 be generic and F⁺_k = {u ∈ ℝ³ : 3 ≤ u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ u₃, u₁² + u₂² + u₃² + u₁u₂u₃ = k}. The points of F⁺_k(ℤ) are pairwise Γ-inequivalent, and every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a unique u′ = (−u₁, u₂, u₃) with u ∈ F⁺_k(ℤ). (ii) Let k < 0 be admissible and F⁻_k = {u ∈ ℝ³ : 3 ≤ u₁ ≤ u₂ ≤ u₃ ≤ u₁u₂/2, u₁² + u₂² + u₃² − u₁u₂u₃ = k}. The points of F⁻_k(ℤ) are pairwise Γ-inequivalent, and every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) is Γ-equivalent to a unique u ∈ F⁻_k(ℤ). In particular h_M(k) = |F^±_k(ℤ)| is finite and computable.
items.locator: Theorem 1.1, pp.3–4; proof §4.1–4.2, pp.12–14, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Existence by Lemmas 2.1–2.2; uniqueness because Δ has a unique minimum on each component of the Vieta tree. Examples: h(3685) = 6, h(−3691) = 9 (re-computed in this extraction). Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 4.1 (the Cayley cubic k = 4)
items.statement: V₄(ℤ) has infinitely many Γ-orbits, each containing exactly one point of the form (2, a, a) with a ≥ 0 (up to permutation and double sign change). The orbit of (2, 0, 0) ∼ (−2, 0, 0) has one element and that of (2, 1, 1) two, and Δ attains a unique minimum on each orbit (Δ(−2,0,0) = 9, Δ(−1,1,1) = −16, Δ(2,a,a) = 9 − 4a²).
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Remark 4.2 (Δ-descent and the asymptotics of Δ)
items.statement: Δ-descent alone gives finiteness of the number of orbits: a positive node either descends to a negative node or starts an infinite strictly Δ-decreasing chain of positive nodes, impossible since Δ ≥ 0 on positive nodes; the at most finitely many negative nodes in S⁺(k) are pairwise inequivalent. As k → ∞, Lagrange multipliers give (without proof in the paper) min_{S⁺(k)} Δ ≥ k² + 18k^{3/2} + 88k + (621/4)k^{1/2} + O(1), max_{S⁻(k)} Δ ≤ k² − 18k^{3/2} + 88k − (45/4)k^{1/2} + O(1), min_{S⁻(k)} Δ ≥ −3k^{4/3} + O(k), so the first h(k) minima of Δ on V_k(ℤ) occur at the roots.
items.note: The three asymptotic bounds are asserted without proof. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Consequences (a)–(c) of Theorem 1.1
items.statement: (a) h_M(46) = 0, and 46 is the smallest positive Hasse failure. (b) h_M(−2) = 1, all solutions being equivalent to (3, 3, 4), and −4 is the largest negative Hasse failure. (c) h_M(k) ≪_ε |k|^{1/3+ε} as k → ±∞, because for fixed x₁ the fundamental set bounds the number of units acting on the indefinite binary quadratic form in (x₂, x₃).
items.note: (a) and (b) were re-verified in this extraction. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 5.1 (reduction of polynomial parametric solutions)
items.statement: For M*(x) = Σ α_jx_j + (β₁x₂x₃ + β₂x₁x₃ + β₃x₁x₂) + x₁² + x₂² + εx₃² − x₁x₂x₃ with ε = ±1 and α_j, β_j ∈ ℤ (5.1): if P_j ∈ ℤ[t] of positive degree satisfy M*(P₁, P₂, P₃) = k identically, then there are q ∈ ℤ and Q₁, Q₂ ∈ ℤ[t] of positive degree with M*(q, Q₁, Q₂) = k identically. Parametric solutions with two constant coordinates do not exist.
items.locator: §5.1, Lemma 5.1 and proof, p.16, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Proof: degree descent by Vieta moves. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Parametric solutions on V_k and on x₁² + x₂² − x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k
items.statement: (1) V_k contains a polynomial parametric integral family iff k − 4 = w² is a square, in which case (2, t, t + w) is one (so a line); in particular there is none for generic k. (2) The surface x₁² + x₂² − x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k has parametric families (of the type (Q₁, Q₂, q)) iff k + 4 = w², e.g. (t + w, t, 2), or k = 0, e.g. (Q, 0, ±Q). By Remark 5.2 this surface has no local obstructions, has the points (0, 2^α(k′ + 1)/2, 2^α(k′ − 1)/2) for k = 4^αk′ with k′ odd, infinitely many integral points when k′ ≠ 1 or α ≥ 3, and infinitely many Hasse failures (for example k = 94), by an argument like Proposition 8.1.
items.note: The Hasse failures in Remark 5.2(iv) are asserted without proof. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Markoff-type affine cubic forms
items.statement: F = F₀ + G with F₀ = c x₁x₂x₃ and G = Σ a_{ij}x_ix_j + Σ a_ix_i + a, where a_{jj} = ±1 and c, a, a_{ij}, a_i ∈ ℤ (1.8), together with their transforms under Aff₃(ℤ). For these the Vieta involutions still act on each V_{k,F}(ℤ). Examples: U₁ = x₁ + x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ (1.9) and U₂ = x₂(x₃ − x₁) + x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ (1.10).
items.note: Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25).

items.name: Parametric families on U₁ and U₂ for every k
items.statement: For every k ∈ ℤ and ε = ±1, (−t² + k − 4ε, −t² + t + k − 4ε, 2) is an integral parametric family on x₁ + x₁² + x₂² + εx₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k. For every k, (−t² + t + k − 1, −t² + k − 1, 1) is one on U₂ = k.
items.note: Verified symbolically in this extraction. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25).

items.name: (1.5): non-empty ⇔ Zariski dense for the Markoff level sets
items.statement: For k ≥ 5 not a square, and for k ≤ 0: V_k(ℤ) ≠ ∅ iff V_k(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_k. Proof: if x̂ ∈ V_k(ℤ) with |x̂₁| ≥ 2, the element (x₁, x₂, x₃) ↦ (x₁, x₁x₂ − x₃, x₂) of Γ preserves the plane x₁ = x̂₁ and acts there by [[x̂₁, −1], [1, 0]] ∈ SL₂(ℤ) of infinite order, so the orbit is infinite and Zariski dense in a curve in the plane x₁ = x̂₁: the slice {x₁ = x̂₁} ∩ V_k is an irreducible conic when |x̂₁| ≥ 3 (k ≠ x̂₁² as k is not a square), and for |x̂₁| = 2 it is the pair of lines (x₂ ∓ x₃)² = k − 4, one or both of which contain the orbit (E20). As in [CZ06], a proper Zariski closure would lie in finitely many curves, allowing only finitely many such x̂₁ (and likewise x̂₂, x̂₃), so V_k(ℤ) would be finite. For |k| > 20 some |x̂_j| ≥ 2; |k| ≤ 20 is checked directly. For squares k the conclusion fails: V₁(ℤ) and V₉(ℤ) are non-empty finite orbits. When k = k₁² with k₁ having an odd prime factor ≡ 1 (mod 4), V_k(ℤ) has an infinite orbit and is Zariski dense.
items.locator: §1, (1.5), p.3; §5.2.1, p.17, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (error E6: the paper also lists k = 49 among the finite cases)
items.note: [CL09, Theorem D] proves a stronger statement about Γ-invariant curves. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25). The printed claim that the closure contains the whole slice fails for |x̂₁| = 2; see E20. [review REV-PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22]

items.name: U₁ and U₂ are perfect and universal
items.statement: V_{k,U₁}(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_{k,U₁} for every k ∈ ℤ, and V_{k,U₂}(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_{k,U₂} for every k, by the parametric families together with the Vieta actions: in the plane x₂ = const the composite V₁V₃ acts on w = (x₁, x₃) by w ↦ Aw + b with A ∈ SL₂(ℤ) of trace x₂² − 2 (for U₁, A = [[x₂² − 1, −x₂], [x₂, −1]], b = (−1, 0)), and for |x₂| ≥ 3 this map has no periodic integral point because (A − I)⁻¹b ∉ ℤ²; similarly for U₂ with the planes x₂ = const and x₁ = const. So these forms represent every k with a Zariski-dense set of integral points; the only perfect forms known to the authors are of type (1.8).
items.locator: §1, p.8; §5.2.2–5.2.3, pp.17–18, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (error E5 in the U₁ argument)
items.note: Statement as corrected in E5: the orbits through the points of the parametric family with |x₂| ≥ 3 supply infinitely many planes. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25).

items.name: Markoff surfaces as relative character varieties
items.statement: The level sets V_k are the relative SL₂-character varieties of π₁(Σ_{1,1}), with k = tr(ρ([a, b])) + 2, and Γ is essentially the mapping class group acting on them ([Gol03]). Finiteness of the number of Γ-orbits on integral points persists for Σ_{g,n} ([Wha20]), but fails when ℤ is replaced by S-integers of a general number ring.
items.note: Context for the orbit questions; not used in the proofs. Routed to the Part II ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff (coalesced with PAPER-MARTIN-25).

items.name: The Fricke trace identity
items.statement: For A, B ∈ SL₂(R) over a commutative ring R: tr(A)² + tr(B)² + tr(AB)² − tr(A)tr(B)tr(AB) = tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) + 2 (6.1). So (tr A, tr B, tr AB) ∈ V_{t+2}(R) with t = tr[A, B].
items.note: Planned: Tau Ceti BelyiMaps Layer 4, item 4, "The Fricke trace identity. For A, B ∈ SL(2,ℝ), tr(ABA⁻¹B⁻¹) = (tr A)² + (tr B)² + (tr AB)² − tr A·tr B·tr(AB) − 2, proved by expanding both sides in the eight matrix entries subject to det A = det B = 1." The paper needs it over ℤ and ℤ/pⁿℤ. The planned proof is a polynomial identity, so the blueprint should state it over an arbitrary commutative ring rather than plan it a second time in CA.4. Neither library has it at the pinned commits. [review REV-PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22] Earlier note: Neither pinned library states it (searched SpecialLinearGroup and Matrix.Trace). Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 6.2 and Corollary 6.3 (explicit solutions modulo p^n, p ≥ 5)
items.statement: For every prime p ≥ 5, n ≥ 1 and t ∈ ℤ there are A, B ∈ SL₂(ℤ/p^nℤ) with tr(A)² + tr(B)² + tr(AB)² − tr(A)tr(B)tr(AB) ≡ t + 2: take B = diag(e, f) with ef ≡ 1 and (e − f, p) = 1, c with c(e − f)² ≡ 1, a = 1, b = 2 − t, d = 1 + bc. Hence M(x) ≡ k (mod p^n) has the solution x₁ ≡ 2 − (k − 4)c, x₂ ≡ e + f, x₃ ≡ e − f + fx₁.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 6.4 (points of x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − αx₁x₂x₃ = β modulo p)
items.statement: For p ≥ 3 the number N_p of solutions modulo p is p² + p(−β/p) if p | α, and p² + 1 + p((α²β − 4)/p)(3 + (β/p)) otherwise. In particular N_p ≥ (p − 2)² − 3 > 0 for p ≥ 5, and N_p > 0 for p = 3 by inspection.
items.locator: Lemma 6.4 and proof, pp.19–20, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Proof with quadratic Gauss sums, S_p(1)² = (−1/p)p. Re-verified for all α, β modulo p ≤ 13. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.1/CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 6.1 (local solubility of the Markoff equation)
items.statement: M(x) ≡ k (mod p^n) is soluble for all primes p and all n ≥ 1 unless k ≡ 3 (mod 4) or k ≡ ±3 (mod 9). Thus V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for all p iff k ≢ 3 (mod 4) and k ≢ ±3 (mod 9).
items.locator: Proposition 6.1; proof §6.1–6.3, pp.18–21, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (errors E2, E3 in the proof)
items.note: For p ≥ 5 via Corollary 6.3 or Hensel lifting of a non-singular point. For p = 3 and p = 2 the proof needs the lifts supplied in E2. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Hensel's lemma over ℤ_p
items.statement: If F ∈ ℤ_p[X] and a ∈ ℤ_p satisfy ‖F(a)‖ < ‖F′(a)‖², then F has a unique root z with ‖z − a‖ < ‖F′(a)‖, and ‖F′(z)‖ = ‖F′(a)‖.
items.note: Mathlib/NumberTheory/Padics/Hensel.lean:461 at 082e2d3. The strong form is what the corrected p = 2, 3 cases (E2) need.

items.name: Square of a quadratic Gauss sum
items.statement: For a nontrivial quadratic multiplicative character χ and a primitive additive character ψ on a finite commutative ring R, gaussSum χ ψ ^ 2 = χ(−1)·|R|.
items.locator: Proof of Lemma 6.4, pp.19–20; Appendix B, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Mathlib/NumberTheory/GaussSum.lean:222 at 082e2d3; the library audit records CA.1 Gauss sums as in Mathlib.

items.name: Lemma 7.1 (points with fixed u₁ = a in the positive fundamental set)
items.statement: For 3 ≤ a ≪ K^{1/3}, the number N_a(K) of (m, n) with a ≤ m ≤ n and a² + m² + n² + amn ≤ K equals log[(√(a−2) + √(a+2))/2]·(K − a²)/√(a² − 4) − E_a(K) + O(√K), where E_a(K) = ((K − a²)/a)·(U√(1 + U²) + arsinh U − U²) with U = a²/(2√(K − a²)) counts the omitted strip 0 ≤ m < a. So E_a(K) ≍ a√K for a ≤ K^{1/4}, and E_a(K) = (K/a)(log(a²/√K) + O(1)) for a ≥ K^{1/4}.
items.locator: §7, Lemma 7.1, pp.21–22, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (error E1: the paper has no E_a term)
items.note: Corrected statement. Checked against exact counts at K = 10^10, a = 10, …, 2000. Routed to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 7.2 (count for the positive fundamental sets)
items.statement: R⁺(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ ≤ K} = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K).
items.locator: §7, Lemma 7.2, p.22, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (error E1: the paper states 1/36)
items.note: Corrected constant. Summing the main term of Lemma 7.1 gives K(log K)²/36, and the strip E_a removes K(log K)²·∫_{1/4}^{1/3}(2t − 1/2)dt = K(log K)²/144. Exact counts for K = 10^6, …, 10^11 fit c₂ = 0.0211. Routed to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 7.3 (count for the negative fundamental sets)
items.statement: R⁻(K) = #{(x₁, x₂, x₃) : 3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃ ≤ x₁x₂/2, 1 ≤ x₁x₂x₃ − x₁² − x₂² − x₃² ≤ K} = (1/48)K(log K)² + O(K log K).
items.note: Stated without details in the paper. Exact counts up to 10^11 fit c₂ = 0.0210, consistent. Routed to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 as a source.

items.name: (1.6): the average of the class numbers
items.statement: Σ_{k ≠ 4, 0 < ±k ≤ K} h^±_M(k) ∼ C_± K(log K)² as K → ∞ with C_± > 0; by Lemmas 7.2–7.3 (as corrected) C₊ = C₋ = 1/48. So h_M(k) has average of order (log |k|)².
items.note: Routed to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 as a source.

items.name: Quadratic reciprocity and the supplementary laws at 2 and −2
items.statement: For distinct odd primes p, q: (q/p)(p/q) = (−1)^{((p−1)/2)((q−1)/2)}; 2 is a square mod an odd prime p iff p ≡ ±1 (mod 8); −2 is a square mod p iff p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8).
items.note: Mathlib/NumberTheory/LegendreSymbol/QuadraticReciprocity.lean:107, :74, :80 at 082e2d3. The residue criteria for 3 and 5 follow by reciprocity.

items.name: Sums of two squares
items.statement: A natural number n is a sum of two squares iff every prime q ≡ 3 (mod 4) divides n to an even power.
items.note: Mathlib/NumberTheory/SumTwoSquares.lean:211 at 082e2d3.

items.name: (8.1): failure of strong approximation modulo 4d
items.statement: Let k = 4 + d, suppose n ↦ (4d/n) is a primitive Dirichlet character mod 4d, and let S_d = {n : (4d/n) ∈ {0, 1}} ⊂ ℤ/4dℤ. Then every x ∈ V_k(ℤ) satisfies x_j² − 4 ∈ S_d (mod 4d) for j = 1, 2, 3, because w² − 4d = (x₁² − 4)(x₂² − 4) with w = 2x₃ − x₁x₂ (8.2) forces (4d/q) ∈ {0, 1} for every prime q | x_j² − 4. By quadratic reciprocity these are congruence conditions on the x_j not implied by local solubility, so strong approximation fails for V_k(ℤ) modulo 4d.
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 8.1 (families of Hasse failures)
items.statement: V_k(ℤ) = ∅ but V_k(ℤ_p) ≠ ∅ for all p in each case: (i) k = 4 − 2ν² < 0 with ν odd and all prime factors of ν ≡ 1 or 3 (mod 8); (ii) k = 4 + 2ν² > 4 with all prime factors of ν ≡ ±1 (mod 8) and ν ≡ 0, ±3, ±4 (mod 9); (iii) k = 4 + 2ℓ² with ℓ ≥ 13 prime, ℓ ≡ ±4 (mod 9) (smallest k = 342). Proof: some x_j is odd, so x_j² − 4 ≡ 5 (mod 8) has a prime factor q ≡ 5, 7 (resp. ±3) (mod 8), and (8.4) makes −2 (resp. 2) a square mod q. In case (iii) the fundamental set of Theorem 1.1 bounds an odd coordinate by √(k/3), which excludes q = ℓ; the non-exceptionality of k is checked separately.
items.locator: Proposition 8.1 and proof, pp.23–24, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (misprint E7 in the proof)
items.note: k = −14, −238, 342 were re-verified. [LM20] and [CTWX20] show that (i) and (ii) are explained by the integral Brauer–Manin obstruction but (iii) is not. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 8.2 (Hasse failures k = 4 + 12ν²)
items.statement: If ν² ≡ 25 (mod 32) and every prime factor of ν is ≡ ±1 (mod 12), then k = 4 + 12ν² is admissible and V_k(ℤ) = ∅. The smallest such ν is 11, with k = 1456.
items.locator: Proposition 8.2 and proof, pp.24–25, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (misprint E8: the paper gives ν = 37, k = 16432)
items.note: Proof: reciprocity for the prime factors of x_j² − 4 via (8.6) when the x_j are odd, a Vieta move when exactly one is even, and congruences modulo 8 and 16 when all are even. k = 1456 and 16432 were re-verified as Hasse failures. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 8.3 (Hasse failures k = 4 + 20ν²)
items.statement: If ν ≡ ±4 (mod 9) and every prime factor of ν is ≡ ±1 (mod 20), then k = 4 + 20ν² is admissible and V_k(ℤ) = ∅; the smallest such ν is 41, with k = 33624.
items.locator: Proposition 8.3 and proof, p.25, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (gap E9, misprint E10 in the proof)
items.note: Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 1.2(i) (infinitely many Hasse failures)
items.statement: The number of Hasse failures with 0 < k ≤ K, and the number with −K ≤ k < 0, are each ≫ K^{1/2}(log K)^{−1/2}. So M is not perfect.
items.locator: Theorem 1.2(i), p.5; proof §8, pp.22–25, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (gap E11: the paper writes "at least √K(log K)^{−1/2}")
items.note: From Proposition 8.1 and the count of integers whose prime factors lie in a set of primes of density 1/2. Routed to ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 as a source.

items.name: Landau-type counts
items.statement: (a) #{0 < k ≤ K : k = u² + v², or 4(k − 1) = u² + 3v², or k − 4 = u²} ≪ K(log K)^{−1/2}; the count of exceptional k is asymptotic to C′K(log K)^{−1/2}. (b) For a set of primes defined by congruence classes and of relative density 1/2 (such as p ≡ 1, 3 (mod 8), or p ≡ ±1 (mod 8)), #{ν ≤ X : every prime factor of ν lies in the set} ≍ X(log X)^{−1/2}, also with a further congruence condition on ν.
items.note: Used, not proved, in the paper; the Landau–Ramanujan and Wirsing/Selberg–Delange theorems. Neither pinned library has them. Routed to AnalyticNumberTheory AN.5 as a source.

items.name: The tentacled sectors and the counting functions r_a, b_𝒜
items.statement: Parameters: K → ∞, (log K)² < A ≪_ε K^ε, 𝒜 = [√A, A], m = ∏_{p ≤ L} p^B with L = (log A/log log A)Φ(A), B = log log A/Φ(A)², Φ(A) = ½√(log log A/log log log A), so m = A^{(1 + o(1))/Φ(A)}. For a ∈ 𝒜: g_a(x₁, x₂) = x₁² + x₂² + ax₁x₂, f_a = g_a + a² (9.1), D_a = a² − 4, and the sector S_d = {s₁, s₂ ≥ 0, 0 ≤ s₁² − ds₂² ≤ 1, 2√d s₂ ≤ s₁ ≤ 3√d s₂} (9.2), of area C/√d with C = (1/4)log(3/2) (constants 1/3, 1/2 for k < 0, Remark 9.1). R_d(k) counts lattice points of √K S_d on G_d = k with a parity condition (9.3); r_a(k) = #{(x₁, x₂) ∈ √(4K)S_{D_a} ∩ ℤ² : f_a(x₁, x₂) = k}; b_𝒜(k) = Σ_{a ∈ 𝒜} r_a(k) (9.4). A point counted by b_𝒜(k) is a point of x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = k with x₃ = a small.
items.locator: §9, pp.25–27, (9.1)–(9.4), Remark 9.1, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (misprint E14 in the parity condition)
items.note: The "moving plane" region of Remark 1.3(d), which keeps the cusps of the fundamental sets. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemmas 9.2–9.3, Corollary 9.4 and the mean value (9.5)
items.statement: Σ_{k ≤ K} R_d(k) = CK/(2√d) + O_ε(K^{1/2+ε}); uniformly in α₁, α₂, Σ_{x ≡ α (mod m), f_a(x) ≤ K, x ∈ √(4K)S_{D_a}} 1 = 2CK/(√(D_a)m²) + O_ε(K^{3/4+ε}); Σ_{k ≤ K} r_a(k) = 2CK/√(D_a) + O_ε(K^{1/2+ε}); and Σ_{k ≤ K} b_𝒜(k) = CK log A + O(KA^{−1/2}), so b_𝒜(k) has mean value C log A.
items.locator: Lemmas 9.2–9.3, Corollary 9.4, (9.5), pp.26–27, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (misprint E12 in (9.5))
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Local densities, singular series and truncated densities
items.statement: For an affine variety V over ℤ in n variables with one equation, δ_p(V) = lim_{ν→∞} #V(ℤ/p^νℤ)/p^{ν(n−1)} and δ(V) = ∏_p δ_p(V). Here: δ(V_k) = ∏_p δ_p(V_k) for (9.6), δ_p(a₁, a₂) for V_{a₁,a₂} : f_{a₁}(x) = f_{a₂}(y) (9.18)–(9.19), and the truncations δ^{(m)}(k) = #V_k(ℤ/mℤ)/m² (9.7), δ^{(m)}(a₁, a₂) = #V_{a₁,a₂}(ℤ/mℤ)/m³ (9.22), δ_m(V^{(2)}) for V^{(2)} : x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₁x₂x₃ = y₁² + y₂² + y₃² + y₁y₂y₃ (9.10). With N_l as in (B.1), δ_p = 1 + Σ_{l ≥ 1} N_l (B.2).
items.note: ES.3 plans p-adic local densities as limits of counts modulo p^k and singular series with Euler factorisation; the library audit records both as absent.

items.name: The variance and its expansion
items.statement: V(K) = V(K, A, m) = Σ_{k ≤ K}(b_𝒜(k) − C(log A)δ^{(m)}(k))² (9.8) = Σ₁ + Σ₂ + Σ₃, with Σ₃ = C²(log A)²(K + O(m))δ_m(V^{(2)}) (9.9) and Σ₂ = −2C²K((log A)² + O(A^{−1/2}log A))δ_m(V^{(2)}) (9.11)–(9.14), by Lemma 9.3 and periodicity of δ^{(m)} modulo m; Σ₁ = Σ_a Σ_k r_a(k)² + Σ_{a₁ ≠ a₂} Σ_k r_{a₁}(k)r_{a₂}(k) (9.15).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Blomer–Granville bound for representation numbers ([BG06, Theorem 2])
items.statement: For positive-definite binary quadratic forms, the number of (s₁, s₂, t₁, t₂) with s₁² + dt₂² = s₂² + dt₁², s_j ≪ K^{1/2}, t_j ≪ (K/d)^{1/2} is ≪ K/√d + K(log K)τ(d)/d, with absolute implied constants.
items.locator: Proof of Lemma 9.5, p.29, citing Blomer–Granville [BG06, Theorem 2], arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: An imported estimate for counts of representations by binary forms in boxes. Routed to GeometryOfNumbersAndQuadraticArithmetic GN.4 as a source.

items.name: Lemma 9.5 (the diagonal terms)
items.statement: (a) Σ_{k ≤ K} R_d(k)² ≪ K/√d + K log K τ(d)/d; (b) Σ_{a ∈ 𝒜} Σ_{k ≤ K} r_a(k)² ≪ K log A, with absolute implied constants.
items.locator: Lemma 9.5 and proof, p.29, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: (a) by switching t₁ and t₂ and applying [BG06, Theorem 2]; (b) as Lemma 9.3 follows from 9.2, using (log K)² ≪ A. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: (9.17): Kloosterman's method for the off-diagonal terms
items.statement: For a₁ ≠ a₂ in 𝒜, Σ_{k ≤ K} r_{a₁}(k)r_{a₂}(k) = δ^{(K)}_∞(a₁, a₂)δ_fin(a₁, a₂) + O(K^{1−ε₀}) for some ε₀ > 0, uniformly in a₁, a₂ ∈ 𝒜: an asymptotic count of weighted integral points on the quaternary quadratic equation f_{a₁}(x) = f_{a₂}(y) in the region √(4K)S_{a₁} × √(4K)S_{a₂}, with singular integral δ^{(K)}_∞ and singular series δ_fin = ∏_p δ_p(a₁, a₂).
items.locator: §9, (9.17)–(9.19), p.30, citing Heath-Brown [HB96] and Niedermowwe [Nie10], arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Imported from the δ-method (Kloosterman refinement) for quadratic forms with weights, with uniformity in the varying forms. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: (9.20): the singular integral
items.statement: δ^{(K)}_∞(a₁, a₂) = ∫_ℝ ∫_{ℝ⁴} χ_{a₁,a₂}(x, y) e(t(g_{a₁}(x) − g_{a₂}(y) + a₁² − a₂²)) dx dy dt = lim_{ε→0} ε^{−1} vol{(x, y) ∈ √(4K)S_{a₁,a₂} : |g_{a₁}(x) − g_{a₂}(y) + a₁² − a₂²| < ε} = (4C²K/(a₁a₂))(1 + O(A^{−1})).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: (9.21)–(9.29): replacing δ_fin by δ^{(m)} and the main term of Σ₁
items.statement: Σ₁ = 4C²K(1 + O(A^{−1}))Σ_{a₁ ≠ a₂} δ_fin(a₁, a₂)/(a₁a₂) + O(K log A + K^{1−ε₀}A²) (9.21). Replacing δ_fin by δ^{(m)} costs O((log A)² min(L, 2^B)^{−1/2}) from the s = gcd(D_{a₁}, D_{a₂}) in S_{A,m} = {s with a prime factor > L or an exponent ≥ B} (9.24)–(9.25), and O(K min(Φ(A), 2^B)^{−1}(log A)²) from the other s. Here δ_p(a₁, a₂) = 1 + O(p^{−2}) for p ∤ D_{a₁}D_{a₂}(D_{a₁} − D_{a₂}), and δ_p = δ_p^{(m)} + O(p^{−B}) (Propositions B.4–B.5, Corollary B.15). With Φ(A)² ≪ 2^B = o(L), Σ₁ = 4C²KΣ_{a₁ ≠ a₂} δ^{(m)}(a₁, a₂)/(a₁a₂) + O(KΦ(A)^{−1}(log A)²) = C²K(log A)²δ_m(V^{(2)}) + O(KΦ(A)^{−1}(log A)²) (9.28)–(9.29).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Proposition 9.6 (the variance estimate)
items.statement: As K → ∞, with (log K)² < A ≪_ε K^ε, 𝒜 = [√A, A] and Φ(A) = ½√(log log A/log log log A): Σ_{k ≤ K}[b_𝒜(k) − C(log A)δ^{(m)}(k)]² ≪ KΦ(A)^{−1}(log A)².
items.note: The main terms of Σ₁, Σ₂, Σ₃ are C²K(log A)²δ_m(V^{(2)}) times 1, −2 and 1, and cancel. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Remark 9.7 (removing the parameter B)
items.statement: δ^{(m)}(k) = ∏_{p ≤ L} δ_p(k) + O(2^{−B}), since δ^{(m)}(k) = ∏_{p ≤ L} δ^{(m)}_p(k) with δ^{(m)}_p(k) = 1 + Σ_{1 ≤ l ≤ B} N_l(k) = δ_p(k) + O(p^{−B}) (Propositions B.1–B.2).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: §9.1: δ^{(m)}(k) is rarely small
items.statement: For admissible k, δ^{(m)}(k) ≫ ∏_{5 ≤ p ≤ L}(1 + χ_p(k − 4)(3 + χ_p(k))/p) + o(1) (9.32), the factors at p = 2, 3 being bounded below for admissible k. Expanding [δ^{(m)}(k)]^{−1} ≪ Σ_{n ≤ M} μ(n)A(k, n)/n with A(k, p) = χ_p(k − 4)(3 + χ_p(k)) for p ≥ 5 (9.33)–(9.34), and using Σ_{k mod p} A(k, p) = −1, gives Σ_{k ≤ K admissible}[δ^{(m)}(k)]^{−1} ≪ K. Hence #{0 ≤ k ≤ K admissible : δ^{(m)}(k) < ε} ≪ εK for every ε > 0 (9.36).
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Theorem 1.2(ii) (M is almost perfect)
items.statement: #{|k| ≤ K : k admissible, h_M(k) = 0} = o(K) as K → ∞, and for almost all admissible k, V_k(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_k. So M is full and almost perfect.
items.locator: Theorem 1.2(ii), p.7; proof §9, pp.25–34, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version)
items.note: Chebyshev with Proposition 9.6 and (9.36) gives b_𝒜(k) > 0 for almost all admissible k; Zariski density then follows from (1.5). The case k < 0 is analogous (Remark 9.1). Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Remark 1.3(c) (h(k) → ∞ for almost all generic k)
items.statement: For each fixed t ≥ 0, #{0 ≤ |k| ≤ K : h_M(k) = t, k generic} = o(K) as K → ∞. So h_M(k) → ∞ as k runs through almost all generic k.
items.note: From the proof of Theorem 1.2(ii) combined with Theorem 1.1. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Arithmetic invariants of affine cubic forms (Appendix A)
items.statement: The h-invariant h(f) of [DL64]: the least h with f₀ = L₁Q₁ + … + L_hQ_h (L_j linear, Q_j quadratic forms over ℚ); n − h(f) is the dimension of the largest rational linear subspace in f₀ = 0, and h(f) = 1 iff f₀ is reducible over ℚ. l(f), q(f): the dimensions of the largest rational affine subspaces on which f restricts to a non-constant linear, resp. quadratic, function; h(f) = 1 iff q(f) = n − 1 (A.2). These are invariant under Aff_n(ℤ); for n = 3 generic f have 9 invariants up to the constant term (I(f₀), J(f₀) and the quadratic part). Examples: h(S) = 3, l(S) = q(S) = 0 for S = x₁³ + x₂³ + x₃³; h(M) = 1, l(M) = 0, q(M) = 2; T = x₁x₂x₃ + x₁ + x₂ has h = 1, l = q = 2, v_T(k) = ∞ but T is not almost perfect; P = x₁x₂x₃ + (x₁ − 1)Q₁ + (x₂ − 1)Q₂ has l = q = 1 and V_{k,P}(ℤ) ≠ ∅ for all k.
items.note: Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Fullness beyond M (stated, proofs deferred)
items.statement: If F₀ is reducible over ℚ (h(F) = 1) then F is full, by the moving-plane method with the rational plane in F₀ = 0. If F₀ is irreducible, a natural circle-method hypothesis in the spirit of [Hoo16] on the count of points on F(x) = F(y) with (x, y) ∈ R × R, for tentacled regions R near the curve F₀ = 0 in ℙ²(ℝ), would make F full, in particular F = S (the sum of three cubes).
items.note: Proofs are deferred to a forthcoming paper; statement-level endpoints only. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source.

items.name: Propositions B.1–B.2, (B.6) and Remark B.3 (δ_p(k) for odd p)
items.statement: For p ≥ 3 and N_l(k) as in (B.1): N₁(k) = χ(k − 4)[3 + χ(k)]/p + 1/p²; for odd l ≥ 3, N_l(k) = 4p^{−(l+1)/2}χ((k − 4)/p^{l−1}) if p^{l−1} | k − 4, and ε_p p^{−(l+1)/2}χ(k/p^{l−1}) if p^{l−1} | k, with ε_p = χ(−1) = (−1/p); for even l ≥ 2, N_l(k) = −p^{−(l+2)/2}{4η_{l−1}(k − 4) + η_{l−1}(k)} if p^{l−1} ∥ k(k − 4), p^{−l/2}(1 − 1/p){4η_l(k − 4) + η_l(k)} if p^l | k(k − 4), and 0 otherwise. So if p^μ ∥ k(k − 4): μ = 0 gives δ_p(k) = 1 + χ(k − 4)(3 + χ(k))/p + 1/p²; p ∥ k gives 1 + 3χ(−1)/p; p ∥ k − 4 gives 1 − 3/p²; μ ≥ 2 gives the formulas of Proposition B.2(d)–(e), with χ((k − 4)/p^μ) in (e) and, for even μ in (d), 1 − χ(−k/p^μ) in place of 1 − χ(k/p^μ); these differ from the printed formulas exactly when p ≡ 3 (mod 4). In particular δ₃(k) = 0 iff k ≡ 3, 6 (mod 9).
items.locator: Appendix B.1, (B.1)–(B.6), Propositions B.1–B.2, Remark B.3, pp.45–47, arXiv:1706.06712v3 (final version) (error E15 and misprint E16)
items.note: Corrected statement. Checked against direct counts modulo 3^7, 5^5 and 7^4. Routed to ExponentialSumsAndCircleMethod ES.3/ES.4 as a source. The sign correction applies to every p ≡ 3 (mod 4), not only p = 3: direct counts give δ₇(49) = 34/49, δ₇(147) = 36/49, δ₁₁(121) = 98/121 and δ₁₁(242) = 100/121 (printed 36/49, 34/49, 100/121, 98/121), and N₃(49) = −1/49 at p = 7 (printed +1/49); p = 5 and p = 13 agree with the printed formulas (E15). [review REV-PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22]

items.name: Propositions B.4–B.5 and Remark B.6 (δ_p(a₁, a₂) for odd p)
items.statement: For a₁ ≠ a₂ and p ≥ 3, with p^{η_i} ∥ D_{a_i}, η = min(η₁, η₂) and p^μ ∥ D_{a₁} − D_{a₂}: (a) if p ∤ D_{a₁}D_{a₂}(D_{a₁} − D_{a₂}) then δ_p(a₁, a₂) = 1 − χ(D_{a₁}D_{a₂})/p²; (b) if p ∤ D_{a₁}D_{a₂} and μ ≥ 1 then δ_p = (1 + 1/p)(1 − p^{−μ−1}); (c) if p | D_{a₁}D_{a₂} and p ∤ D_{a₁} − D_{a₂} then δ_p = 1 + 1/p; (d) if η₁, η₂, μ ≥ 1 then δ_p = (1 + η) − (η − 1)/p if η₁ ≠ η₂, (1 + η) − η/p − χ(D_{a₁}/p^η)χ(D_{a₂}/p^η)/p² if η₁ = η₂ = μ, and (1 + η) − (η − 1)/p − p^{−(μ−η+1)}(1 + 1/p) if η₁ = η₂ < μ. The individual N_l(a₁, a₂) of Proposition B.4 are as stated in (a)–(c) and for η₁ ≠ η₂; for η₁ = η₂ = μ, N_{η+1} = −p^{−η−1}χχ, and for η₁ = η₂ < μ, N_{η+j} = p^{−j}(1 − 1/p) for 1 ≤ j ≤ μ − η and N_{μ+1} = −p^{−(μ−η+2)}. Remark B.6: δ_p(a, a) = 1 + 1/p if p ∤ D_a, and (1 + η) − (η − 1)/p if p^η ∥ D_a.

items.name: Lemmas B.7–B.10 and Proposition B.12 (the 2-adic factor δ₂(k))
items.statement: Lemma B.7 evaluates the quadratic Gauss sums F_l(c) = Σ_{x mod 2^l} e(cx²/2^l) and their twisted sums; Lemma B.8 the two-variable sums Q_l(b; a); Lemmas B.9–B.10 give N₀ = 1, N₁(k) = (−1)^k/4, N₂(k) = cos(kπ/2)/4 + 3 sin(kπ/2)/4, N₃, N₄, N₅ and N_l for l ≥ 6. Consequently, for k ≠ 0, 4, δ₂(k) = 0 iff k ≡ 3 (mod 4), and otherwise δ₂(k) ≥ 3/4. For odd k ≡ 1 (mod 4), δ₂(k) = (3/8)(1 + χ₄(k))(2 − χ₈(k)), which is 3/4 for k ≡ 1 (mod 8) and 9/4 for k ≡ 5 (mod 8); δ₂(k) = 1 if 2 ∥ k.

items.name: Lemma B.13, Proposition B.14 and Corollary B.15 (the 2-adic factor δ₂(a₁, a₂))
items.statement: For a₁ ≠ ±a₂ and a_j ≠ ±2: if a₁, a₂ are odd and 2^η ∥ D_{a₁} − D_{a₂} with η ≥ 3, then δ₂(a₁, a₂) = (3/2)(1 − 2^{−η−1}) (B.10); if a₁ is even and a₂ odd, with 2^θ ∥ a₁²/4 − 1, then δ₂(a₁, a₂) = 5/4 if θ = 0 and 3/2 if θ ≥ 3; for both even, Proposition B.14(3) lists the N_l. routes.reason: CA.4 owns classical Diophantine equations and elementary descent, and must preserve local-solubility conditions and prove a bound before a finite search counts as complete. PAPER-MARTIN-25 already sources the coefficient-three Markoff equation, the Vieta involutions and the descent to (1,1,1) there, and that route is accepted. This paper extends the same carrier to every level set x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ = k. It gives the descent Lemmas 2.1–2.2, the Δ-function, the fundamental sets of Theorem 1.1 and finiteness and computability of h(k), and the Cayley cubic. It also covers polynomial parametric solutions, local solubility (Proposition 6.1, with the Fricke identity and the Gauss-sum count of Lemma 6.4, which rests on CA.1 Gauss sums), the reciprocity obstructions of §8 with Theorem 1.2(i), and the enumeration of §10. All of it is elementary, and none is in either pinned library. Quadratic reciprocity, Gauss sums, Hensel's lemma and sums of two squares are already in Mathlib (library items). The Fricke trace identity is not part of this route: Tau Ceti BelyiMaps Layer 4 plans it (item 23 is planned), and CA.4 imports it. [review REV-PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22]

ES.4 owns Waring-type and forms-in-many-variables endpoints and asks that each optimised endpoint be a separate source theorem, recording variables, degree and error exponent before claiming a Hasse principle. ES.3 owns singular integrals and p-adic local densities, with factorisation and positivity. Theorem 1.2(ii), that almost all admissible k are represented by M, is such an endpoint, in the style of Davenport's almost-all theorem for four cubes. Its proof is a variance argument over moving planes: the tentacled sectors, Lemmas 9.2–9.5, the δ-method asymptotic (9.17) for the quaternary equations f_{a₁}(x) = f_{a₂}(y), the singular integral (9.20), the truncated singular series and Proposition 9.6, and the lower bound (9.36). The explicit local densities δ_p(k) and δ_p(a₁, a₂) of Appendix B are ES.3 inputs; the definition of local densities is planned there. The ES.3 and ES.4 audits record everything as absent. The invariants of Appendix A and the deferred fullness claims belong with the same forms-in-many-variables endpoints.

GN.4 owns lattice-point estimates, with main term and error. The audit marks it partly built: Mathlib has the volume limit for dilated regions but no counts in regions like these. The paper counts lattice points in the tentacled fundamental regions {3 ≤ x₁ ≤ x₂ ≤ x₃, x₁² + x₂² + x₃² ± x₁x₂x₃ ≤ K} (Lemmas 7.1–7.3), giving the average (1.6) of the class numbers. With the correction in E1 both constants are 1/48. It imports the Blomer–Granville bound for the number of representations by binary quadratic forms in boxes. Both are lattice-point estimates for specific quadratic and cubic regions, with explicit dependence on the parameter a or d.

AN.5 owns mean values of multiplicative functions. The paper uses two such results without proof. The first is the Landau-type bound for integers represented by u² + v², by u² + 3v², or of the form 4 + u², used to discard exceptional k. The second is the Landau–Wirsing count of integers whose prime factors lie in a set of primes of relative density 1/2, which gives the order K^{1/2}(log K)^{−1/2} in Theorem 1.2(i). Both are standard Selberg–Delange mean-value theorems. Neither pinned library has them, and no other stage names them.

routes.title: Arithmetic dynamics, Part II: Markoff actions and strong approximation
routes.reason: PAPER-MARTIN-25 proposed this Part II, it was accepted, and DESIGN-ArithmeticDynamicsPartIIMarkoff is pending. It extends ArithmeticDynamics by affine polynomial group actions on Markoff surfaces, which DY.0–DY.6 do not cover. This paper adds the integral-point side of those actions. It shows that Γ-orbits on the level sets V_k(ℤ) are Zariski dense (1.5), and that the Vieta dynamics of the Markoff-type forms U₁, U₂ make them perfect and universal. It also explains V_k as relative character varieties with Γ the mapping class group. These are not classical Diophantine statements, and they need the same Vieta-action carriers, so they coalesce with that Part II rather than open a second one. No item of PAPER-MARTIN-25 is duplicated.
routes.brief:
Coalesces with the brief of PAPER-MARTIN-25; this adds integral level sets. Import from ClassicalArithmeticCompletion CA.4 (as sourced by PAPER-MARTIN-25 and PAPER-GHOSH-SARNAK-22): the coefficient-one Markoff cubic M = x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃, its level sets V_k, the group Γ generated by the Vieta involutions, permutations and double sign changes, and the fundamental sets of Ghosh–Sarnak Theorem 1.1. Keep the normalisations apart: V₀(ℤ) \ {0} = 3·(coefficient-three Markoff triples), and do not transport the p = 3 statements of PAPER-MARTIN-25 through this rescaling.

Final theorems. (1) For k ≥ 5 not a square and for k ≤ 0, V_k(ℤ) ≠ ∅ iff V_k(ℤ) is Zariski dense in V_k. Prove it via the SL₂(ℤ) action [[x̂₁, −1], [1, 0]] on conic slices {x₁ = x̂₁} ∩ V_k, irreducibility of the slices for non-square k, and the Corvaja–Zannier finiteness argument, with the finite check for |k| ≤ 20. (2) For squares k: V₁(ℤ) and V₉(ℤ) are finite single orbits, V₄₉(ℤ) contains the infinite orbit of (1, 4, 8), and V_{k₁²}(ℤ) is Zariski dense when k₁ has an odd prime factor ≡ 1 mod 4. (3) Markoff-type forms F = c x₁x₂x₃ + G with a_{jj} = ±1 and their Aff₃(ℤ) transforms carry Vieta actions. U₁ = x₁ + x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ and U₂ = x₂(x₃ − x₁) + x₁² + x₂² + x₃² − x₁x₂x₃ have integral parametric families for every k, and V_{k,U₁}(ℤ), V_{k,U₂}(ℤ) are Zariski dense for every k, so U₁, U₂ are perfect and universal. Use the affine maps w ↦ Aw + b on planes x₂ = const with A = [[x₂² − 1, −x₂], [x₂, −1]] for U₁, and orbits through family points with |x₂| ≥ 3 (A hyperbolic, (A − I)⁻¹b ∉ ℤ²). (4) Record, as a statement-level interface, V_k as the relative SL₂-character varieties of the once-punctured torus with Γ the mapping class group action (Goldman), via the Fricke identity sourced in CA.4.

Mandatory regressions: the base points (k − 4, k − 4, 2) of U₁ have V₁V₃-orbits of size 3 for k = 3, 5, so the printed argument fails there; (−1, 2, 0) on U₁ with k = 4 has a parabolic A but an infinite orbit; M(1, 4, 8) = 49 and V₁(1, 4, 8) = (31, 4, 8). Every definition gets evaluation and naturality API, and the Zariski-density statements are proved over ℚ-varieties with explicit irreducible components.
